Traditionally, journal reputation has served two purposes simultaneously: helping researchers locate potentially relevant work and providing a preliminary signal of its quality. Search engines and repositories partially replace the first function by allowing researchers to discover individual articles through keywords, abstracts, citations, and topic recommendations.

However, discovery does not automatically eliminate dependence on reputation. Once researchers encounter an unfamiliar article, they must still decide whether it deserves attention. Their willingness to bypass journal prestige should depend on the availability of alternative information.

For example, an article with a detailed abstract, accessible full text, transparent methods, and linked data gives readers several ways to assess its value. An article with a vague abstract and inaccessible methods leaves readers more dependent on external signals, including journal reputation.

- For unfamiliar or interdisciplinary topics, researchers will continue to rely more heavily on journal reputation, even when search access is equal.

3. The richness of the article information available.
4. The article’s position in the results.

The decline of journal gatekeeping could coexist with stronger platform gatekeeping. Assessing whether scholarly communication is becoming more open would therefore require examining ranking transparency, coverage, and attention allocation, alongside journal prestige and access.

| Function | Possible indicators |

| Discussion | Scholarly commentary, bookmarks, public discussion |
